specAnchors.text: understand that plants can reproduce asexually by natural methods (illustrated by runners) and by artificial methods (illustrated by cuttings)

primer.text: Gardeners cheat time: a strawberry patch doubles itself without a single seed, and a prized rose is copied stem by stem. This note covers both routes — the runner, a plant's own side branch that roots itself, and the cutting, a human-operated clone kit that turns one good plant into many identical ones.

modules.title: Cloning Without a Seed
modules.opening: Asexual reproduction in plants needs one parent only: no gametes meet, no pollen flies, and every offspring is a genetic clone of that parent, whether the plant grows the new individual itself or a gardener helps.
keyPoints: Asexual reproduction involves one parent only.
All offspring are exact genetic copies of the parent — they are clones.
The cloning can happen naturally, as with runners, or artificially, as with cuttings.

low.restatement: One parent, no gametes, identical offspring; the plant copies itself by growing new shoots that become new plants.
low.analogy: Photocopying a page instead of retyping it: the copy matches the original exactly.
low.examPointer: Remember the contrast set: natural = runners, artificial = cuttings.

medium.restatement: Because no fertilisation occurs, mitosis alone builds the new plant, so the genome is passed on unshuffled; the offspring differ from the parent only by mutation, if at all.
medium.analogy: A franchise opening identical branches from one blueprint.
medium.examPointer: Use the word clone explicitly — the mark scheme looks for genetically identical offspring.

modules.title: Runners and Cuttings
sourceHeadings: Natural asexual reproduction in plants – runners
Artificial asexual reproduction in plants – cuttings
modules.opening: Runners and cuttings both end in cloned plants, but one is grown by the plant itself and one is assembled by a gardener: a runner is a sideways stem carrying plantlets that root where they touch soil, while a cutting is a sliced stem, often dipped in rooting powder, that grows its own roots.
keyPoints: Runners are horizontal stems growing sideways from the parent with small plantlets at their ends.
Plantlets grow roots once they touch the soil and become independent new plants.
Cuttings are sections cut from good parent plants, usually bearing a new bud.
A cutting can root in water or soil, sometimes dipped in rooting powder first.
Cloning by cuttings is cheap and quick for gardeners.

low.restatement: The plant sends out a sideways stem that roots itself; the gardener snips a stem and roots it in water or soil.
low.analogy: One method is the plant laying its own railway sleepers; the other is the gardener laying them for it.
low.examPointer: Quote runner for natural and cutting for artificial — the spec names both illustrations.

medium.restatement: Both routes work because stems carry meristem tissue able to sprout roots; rooting powder simply adds plant growth regulators that push root development along faster.
medium.analogy: A cutting with rooting powder is a stem given a head start on its root apprenticeship.
medium.examPointer: Mention the bud on the cutting and the rooting powder option — both score points in method questions.

glossary.definition: A horizontal stem growing sideways from a parent plant, carrying plantlets that root independently.
A tiny new plant formed at the end of a runner, genetically identical to the parent.
A section of stem cut from a parent plant and grown into a new clone.
Powder containing plant growth regulators that encourage a cutting to grow roots.
